claims.claim: Neuromodulators have long been implicated in adapting the retina to different contextual states necessary to robustly perform in a highly dynamic visual environment.
claims.source: Neuromodulators have long been implicated in adapting the retina to different contextual states necessary to robustly perform in a highly dynamic visual environment (e.g. Flood et al., 2018; Goel and Mangel, 2021; Herrmann et al., 2011; Jacoby et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about neuromodulator function supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Dopamine is released by a distinct type of amacrine cell.
claims.source: For instance, dopamine (DA) is released by a distinct type of AC (Bauer et al., 1980; Djamgoz and Wagner, 1992; Godley and Wurtman, 1988; Pérez-Fernández et al., 2019), and has been shown to regulate light adaptation (Flood et al., 2018; Nichols et al., 1967; Nir et al., 2000) via several cellular mechanisms, such as modulation of gap junctional coupling (Goel and Mangel, 2021; Jin and Ribelayga, 2016; Kothmann et al., 2009; Ribelayga et al., 2008) and intrinsic conductances (Hayashida et al., 2009; Lasater and Dowling, 1985).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about dopamine sources in the retina.

claims.claim: Dopamine has been shown to regulate light adaptation via several cellular mechanisms, such as modulation of gap junctional coupling and intrinsic conductances.
claims.source: For instance, dopamine (DA) is released by a distinct type of AC (Bauer et al., 1980; Djamgoz and Wagner, 1992; Godley and Wurtman, 1988; Pérez-Fernández et al., 2019), and has been shown to regulate light adaptation (Flood et al., 2018; Nichols et al., 1967; Nir et al., 2000) via several cellular mechanisms, such as modulation of gap junctional coupling (Goel and Mangel, 2021; Jin and Ribelayga, 2016; Kothmann et al., 2009; Ribelayga et al., 2008) and intrinsic conductances (Hayashida et al., 2009; Lasater and Dowling, 1985).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple cited references about dopamine's mechanisms of action.

claims.claim: Histamine was proposed to shape the retinal code in a top-down modulatory manner related to the animal's arousal state.
claims.source: More recently, histamine was proposed to shape the retinal code in a top-down modulatory manner related to the animal's arousal state (Gastinger et al., 2006; Warwick et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about histamine's role in the retina.

claims.claim: Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) is considered the dominant enzyme producing NO relevant for retinal signal processing.
claims.source: Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) is considered the dominant enzyme producing NO relevant for retinal signal processing, and – depending on species – was shown to be present in different retinal cell classes (Blom et al., 2009; Blute et al., 2000; Blute et al., 1997; Bredt et al., 1990; Dawson et al., 1991; Eldred and Blute, 2005; Palamalai et al., 2006; Yamamoto et al., 1993a; Yamamoto et al., 1993b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about nNOS in the retina.

claims.claim: In the mouse retina, nNOS was mainly found in specific amacrine cell types.
claims.source: In the mouse retina, nNOS was mainly found in specific AC types (Blom et al., 2012; Giove et al., 2009; Haverkamp and Wässle, 2000; Jacoby et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about nNOS localization in mouse retina.

claims.claim: One type of nNOS-containing amacrine cell (nNOS-2 AC) controls the light-dependent release of NO in the inner retina.
claims.source: A few years ago, Jacoby et al., 2018, demonstrated that one of those types (nNOS-2 AC) controls the light-dependent release of NO in the inner retina.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a specific cited reference.

claims.claim: NO can function via two main pathways: binding to NO-GC receptor to trigger cGMP production, and via S-nitrosylation by directly modifying certain receptor and channel proteins.
claims.source: NO can function via two main pathways (Ahern et al., 2002): (i) it can bind to the NO guanylate cyclase (NO-GC; also referred to as soluble guanylate cyclase) receptor, triggering the production of the second messenger cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which binds to downstream targets (Eldred and Blute, 2005; Garthwaite, 2005; Sitaramayya, 2002), and (ii) via S-nitrosylation (cGMP-independent) by directly modifying certain receptor and channel proteins (Hess et al., 2005; Miyagi et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about NO signaling mechanisms.

claims.claim: The effects of NO have been primarily linked with light adaptation and the transition between scotopic and photopic signaling pathways.
claims.source: The effects of NO have been primarily linked with light adaptation and the transition between scotopic and photopic signaling pathways via several mechanisms, including uncoupling the gap junctions between AII ACs and On-cone BCs (Mills and Massey, 1995), increasing the gain of On-cone BCs in response to dim light (Nawy and Jahr, 1990; Snellman and Nawy, 2004), and modulating the gain of Off-cone BCs (Tooker et al., 2013; Vielma et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple cited references about NO's effects on retinal adaptation.

claims.claim: NO uncouples the gap junctions between AII amacrine cells and On-cone bipolar cells.
claims.source: The effects of NO have been primarily linked with light adaptation and the transition between scotopic and photopic signaling pathways via several mechanisms, including uncoupling the gap junctions between AII ACs and On-cone BCs (Mills and Massey, 1995), increasing the gain of On-cone BCs in response to dim light (Nawy and Jahr, 1990; Snellman and Nawy, 2004), and modulating the gain of Off-cone BCs (Tooker et al., 2013; Vielma et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: NO increases the gain of On-cone bipolar cells in response to dim light.
claims.source: The effects of NO have been primarily linked with light adaptation and the transition between scotopic and photopic signaling pathways via several mechanisms, including uncoupling the gap junctions between AII ACs and On-cone BCs (Mills and Massey, 1995), increasing the gain of On-cone BCs in response to dim light (Nawy and Jahr, 1990; Snellman and Nawy, 2004), and modulating the gain of Off-cone BCs (Tooker et al., 2013; Vielma et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: NO modulates the gain of Off-cone bipolar cells.
claims.source: The effects of NO have been primarily linked with light adaptation and the transition between scotopic and photopic signaling pathways via several mechanisms, including uncoupling the gap junctions between AII ACs and On-cone BCs (Mills and Massey, 1995), increasing the gain of On-cone BCs in response to dim light (Nawy and Jahr, 1990; Snellman and Nawy, 2004), and modulating the gain of Off-cone BCs (Tooker et al., 2013; Vielma et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Increasing NO was found to decrease On- and Off-responses in RGCs.
claims.source: At the retina's output level, increasing NO was found to decrease On- and Off-responses in RGCs (Wang et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: Genetically knocking out nNOS led to a reduced light sensitivity in RGCs.
claims.source: Notably, genetically knocking out nNOS also led to a reduced light sensitivity in RGCs (Wang et al., 2007), which was also shown by inhibiting nNOS under light-adapted conditions (Nemargut and Wang, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Inhibiting nNOS under light-adapted conditions led to reduced light sensitivity in RGCs.
claims.source: Notably, genetically knocking out nNOS also led to a reduced light sensitivity in RGCs (Wang et al., 2007), which was also shown by inhibiting nNOS under light-adapted conditions (Nemargut and Wang, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: NO has been shown to modulate RGC responses via cGMP by altering their cGMP-gated conductances.
claims.source: Additionally, NO has been shown to modulate RGC responses via cGMP by altering their cGMP-gated conductances (Ahmad et al., 1994; Kawai and Sterling, 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Approximately one-third of the RGC types displayed highly reproducible, cell type-specific response changes during the course of an experiment in the absence of pharmacological manipulation.
claims.source: When analyzing the control-dataset, we were surprised by finding response changes in the second control measurement 10 min after the first control measurement in approximately one-third of the RGC types in the absence of the NO-donor.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments in the study.

claims.claim: NO had a highly selective effect on a distinct set of three RGC types characterized by their suppressed response to temporal contrast.
claims.source: We found that NO had a highly selective effect on a distinct set of three RGC types characterized by their suppressed response to temporal contrast, where NO strongly and differentially reduced this suppression, as well as caused them to respond faster.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: NO strongly and differentially reduced suppression in contrast-suppressed RGC types and caused them to respond faster.
claims.source: We found that NO had a highly selective effect on a distinct set of three RGC types characterized by their suppressed response to temporal contrast, where NO strongly and differentially reduced this suppression, as well as caused them to respond faster.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: NO had no discernible effects on the spatial receptive field (sRF) properties of contrast-suppressed RGC types.
claims.source: Yet, NO had no discernible effects on their spatial receptive field (sRF) properties.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the receptive field analysis in the study.

claims.claim: NO modulates the visual feature representation of the retinal output in a highly selective and type-specific manner.
claims.source: Together, our data suggest that NO modulates the visual feature representation of the retinal output in a highly selective and type-specific manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Population imaging from somata in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) of ex vivo mouse retina was performed using Oregon Green BAPTA-1 (OGB-1).
claims.source: To investigate NO effects systematically on the retinal output, we performed population imaging from somata in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) of ex vivo mouse retina electroporated with the synthetic Ca2+ indicator Oregon Green BAPTA-1 (Figure 1a–c; Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: A complementary dataset was recorded using multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings.
claims.source: In addition, we recorded a complementary dataset using multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings.
claims.evidence: This describes an additional experimental approach used in the study.

claims.claim: A set of visual stimuli including full-field chirps, moving bars, and binary dense noise was presented to identify different types of RGCs and detect potential NO-induced response changes.
claims.source: To identify the different types of RGCs and detect potential NO-induced response changes, we presented a set of visual stimuli, including full-field chirps, moving bars (Figure 1d), and binary dense noise (Baden et al., 2016) (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claims.claim: Retinal responses recorded with two-photon Ca2+ imaging can be systematically affected by experimental factors such as excitation laser-induced activity, photoreceptor bleaching, and temporal filtering due to Ca2+ buffering by the fluorescent indicator.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that retinal responses recorded with two-photon Ca2+ imaging can be systematically affected by experimental factors, such as excitation laser-induced activity, photoreceptor bleaching, and temporal filtering due to Ca2+ buffering by the fluorescent indicator (Euler et al., 2019; Euler et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about technical considerations in two-photon imaging.

claims.claim: After placing the tissue into the recording chamber, it was allowed to recover from the electroporation for 15 min.
claims.source: After placing the tissue into the recording chamber, it was allowed to recover from the electroporation for 15 min, before we light-adapted the retina for 10 min by presenting the dense noise stimulus.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claims.claim: The retina was light-adapted for 10 min by presenting the dense noise stimulus.
claims.source: After placing the tissue into the recording chamber, it was allowed to recover from the electroporation for 15 min, before we light-adapted the retina for 10 min by presenting the dense noise stimulus.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claims.claim: Each recording field was recorded twice for the complete stimulus set in an interlaced manner.
claims.source: We then selected retinal recording fields, each of which was recorded twice for the complete stimulus set in an interlaced manner (Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claims.claim: The first field was recorded twice without perturbation (control-control).
claims.source: The first field was recorded twice without perturbation (control-control).
claims.evidence: This describes the control condition in the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: For the drug condition, the drug was added to the perfusion medium and the tissue was incubated for approximately 15 min before recording the field for the second time.
claims.source: For the next field, we added the drug to the perfusion medium and incubated the tissue for ∼15 min, before recording the field for the second time (control-drug).
claims.evidence: This describes the drug application protocol in the study.

claims.claim: The time between the first and second recording of field 2 was approximately 15 min longer (the wash-in time) than that of field 1.
claims.source: Note that the time between the first and second recording of field 2 was ∼15 min longer (the wash-in time) than that of field 1 (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: Response quality decreased for the third scan of the same field, likely due to bleaching of fluorescent indicator and photopigment.
claims.source: For the Ca2+ data, we decided against recording also after wash-out, because response quality decreased for the third scan of the same field, likely due to bleaching of fluorescent indicator and photopigment.
claims.evidence: This describes an observation about data quality and a methodological decision.

claims.claim: Wash-out was included in the MEA-dataset.
claims.source: However, we did include wash-out in the MEA-dataset (see below).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological difference between the Ca2+ and MEA datasets.

claims.claim: The sequential-recording protocol yielded paired data at the cell level, allowing tracking of how each cell's responses changed under the drug condition.
claims.source: Our sequential-recording protocol yielded paired data at the cell level, allowing us to track if and how each cell's responses changed under the drug condition.
claims.evidence: This describes the advantage of the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: A total of 3975 RGCs were used in the analyses (nCtrl = 1701; nNO = 1838, nStrychnine = 436).
claims.source: For the following analyses, we used 3975 RGCs (nCtrl = 1701; nNO = 1838, nStrychnine = 436) that fulfilled our response quality filtering (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This provides the sample sizes for the different experimental conditions.

claims.claim: An RGC type classifier was applied to predict a GCL cell's functional type based on soma size and the responses to chirp and moving bar stimuli.
claims.source: As we wanted to investigate if the tested drugs differentially affect the different retinal output channels, we applied an RGC type classifier (Figure 2a; Qiu et al., 2022), which had been trained and validated on a previously published RGC Ca2+ imaging dataset (Baden et al., 2016). The classifier predicts a GCL cell's functional type based on soma size and the responses to chirp and moving bar stimuli (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used for cell type classification.

claims.claim: The classifier also distinguishes between RGCs and displaced amacrine cells.
claims.source: The classifier also distinguishes between RGCs and displaced ACs.
claims.evidence: This describes a capability of the classification method.

claims.claim: Types were predicted based on the responses from the first control recording (Ctrl 1) and the cells retained their type over the course of their experiment.
claims.source: To match the conditions under which the classifier's training data was acquired as closely as possible, we predicted types based on the responses from the first control recording (Ctrl 1) and the cells retained their type over the course of their experiment (no re-typing).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological approach for cell type assignment.

claims.claim: Cells with low confidence scores (< 0.25) were discarded to minimize classification uncertainty.
claims.source: To minimize classification uncertainty, we additionally discarded cells with low confidence scores (< 0.25, see Methods for details).
claims.evidence: This describes a quality control step in the analysis.

claims.claim: The distributions of the predicted RGC types in the datasets matched that of the earlier dataset (Baden et al., 2016) quite well.
claims.source: We found that the distributions of the predicted RGC types in our datasets matched that of the earlier dataset quite well (Figure 2b–d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing the current data to a reference dataset, shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The predicted mean traces for the individual RGC types were very similar to those in Baden et al., 2016.
claims.source: Also, the predicted mean traces for the individual RGC types were very similar to those in Baden et al., 2016 (Figure 2e), as indicated by the high correlations of their chirp and moving bar responses (Figure 2f, left and right, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing response traces to a reference dataset, shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The moving bar responses were more strongly correlated than the chirp responses, likely due to the lower complexity and shorter duration of the moving bar stimulus.
claims.source: That the moving bar responses were more strongly correlated than the chirp responses is likely due to the lower complexity and shorter duration of the former stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data based on stimulus properties.

claims.claim: Glycine is released by small-field amacrine cells in the mouse retina.
claims.source: In the mouse retina, glycine is released by small-field ACs, which relay inhibition vertically across the inner plexiform layer and thus, are involved in cross-over inhibition (Diamond, 2017; Weiss et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about glycinergic signaling in the retina.

claims.claim: Small-field amacrine cells relay inhibition vertically across the inner plexiform layer and are involved in cross-over inhibition.
claims.source: In the mouse retina, glycine is released by small-field ACs, which relay inhibition vertically across the inner plexiform layer and thus, are involved in cross-over inhibition (Diamond, 2017; Weiss et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references about glycinergic signaling in the retina.

claims.claim: Blocking cross-over inhibition between the On- and Off-pathways is expected to have effects on many RGC circuits.
claims.source: Blocking cross-over inhibition between the On- and Off-pathways is therefore expected to have effects on many RGC circuits, which is why we chose the glycine receptor antagonist strychnine to test our recording protocol.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on known circuit organization, used to justify the choice of strychnine as a test drug.

claims.claim: Strychnine revealed additional On-response components in Off and On-Off RGCs.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that strychnine revealed additional On-response components in Off (e.g. G1, G2, G4, G6) and On-Off RGCs (e.g. G11, G12), as can be seen, for instance, in their leading-edge response to the moving bar (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the strychnine experiments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In On RGCs, strychnine did not reveal additional Off response components.
claims.source: In On RGCs, we did not detect additional (Off) response components.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the strychnine experiments.

claims.claim: Some On RGCs exhibited slightly more sustained responses to light increments after strychnine application.
claims.source: Instead, some On RGCs exhibited slightly more sustained responses to light increments (e.g. G18, G20, G22).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the strychnine experiments.

claims.claim: The strychnine-dataset demonstrates that drug-related effects on light responses can be resolved at the RGC type-level.
claims.source: Together, the strychnine-dataset demonstrates that we can resolve drug-related effects on light responses at the RGC type-level.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the strychnine experiments.

claims.claim: The majority of RGC types featured stable responses between Ctrl 1 and Ctrl 2.
claims.source: Surprisingly, while the majority of RGC types featured stable responses (e.g. G1, G21; Figure 3a), a substantial number of RGC types (9/21) changed their responses to chirp and/or moving bar stimuli in the absence of any pharmacological perturbation in a highly reproducible manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments, shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: A substantial number of RGC types (9/21) changed their responses to chirp and/or moving bar stimuli in the absence of any pharmacological perturbation in a highly reproducible manner.
claims.source: Surprisingly, while the majority of RGC types featured stable responses (e.g. G1, G21; Figure 3a), a substantial number of RGC types (9/21) changed their responses to chirp and/or moving bar stimuli in the absence of any pharmacological perturbation in a highly reproducible manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments, shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: G23 showed reduced responses in Ctrl 2.
claims.source: For instance, for Ctrl 2, G23 showed reduced responses, whereas G31 showed an increased response activity (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from the control experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: G31 showed increased response activity in Ctrl 2.
claims.source: For instance, for Ctrl 2, G23 showed reduced responses, whereas G31 showed an increased response activity (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from the control experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: 'Off' RGC types displayed stable responses between control recordings.
claims.source: Interestingly, cells assigned to the functional groups of 'Off' RGC types displayed stable responses, whereas 'On-Off', 'Fast On', 'Slow On', and 'Uncertain RGCs' included types with changing responses (50% (2/4), 34% (1/3), 67% (4/6), and 67% (2/3), respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the control experiments by functional group.

claims.claim: 'On-Off', 'Fast On', 'Slow On', and 'Uncertain RGCs' included types with changing responses (50%, 34%, 67%, and 67%, respectively).
claims.source: Interestingly, cells assigned to the functional groups of 'Off' RGC types displayed stable responses, whereas 'On-Off', 'Fast On', 'Slow On', and 'Uncertain RGCs' included types with changing responses (50% (2/4), 34% (1/3), 67% (4/6), and 67% (2/3), respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the control experiments by functional group.

claims.claim: The diversity of response changes argues against a systematic effect and for a cell type-specific phenomenon.
claims.source: This diversity argues against a systematic effect (such as, e.g., general run-down) and for a cell type-specific phenomenon, which in the following we refer to as 'adaptational response changes'.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the control experiment findings.

claims.claim: The majority of RGC types displayed stable responses during NO application.
claims.source: Similar to the control-dataset, the majority of RGC types displayed stable responses (e.g. G2, G17; Figure 3c), while ∼43% changed their responses significantly (e.g. G28, G32; Figure 3d) following the NO perfusion.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the NO experiments, shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Approximately 43% of RGC types changed their responses significantly following NO perfusion.
claims.source: Similar to the control-dataset, the majority of RGC types displayed stable responses (e.g. G2, G17; Figure 3c), while ∼43% changed their responses significantly (e.g. G28, G32; Figure 3d) following the NO perfusion.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the NO experiments, shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The percentage of changing types per functional group was similar between the control-dataset and NO-dataset.
claims.source: We found that the percentage of changing types per functional group was similar to that in the control-dataset: 'Off' (0% (0/5)), 'On-Off' (50% (2/4)), 'Fast On' (34% (1/3)), 'Slow On' (66% (4/6)), and 'Uncertain RGCs' (66% (2/3)).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing the control and NO datasets.

claims.claim: Only two RGC types (G32 and G18) showed significantly different response changes between control and NO conditions.
claims.source: We, therefore, tested for each RGC type if the response changes observed for control (ΔCtrl: ΔRCtrl2-Ctrl1) and NO (ΔDETA/NO: ΔRNO-Ctrl1) were significantly different (Figure 3e). To our surprise, this was only the case for two types: (1) G32 ('Off suppressed 2') RGC, which is characterized by a high baseline activity that is strongly suppressed below baseline during light increments and displays increased activity during light decrements, and (2) G18, which is considered as being a 'Fast On' type having a response to light increments with a fast response kinetic.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of control and NO datasets, shown in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: G32 ('Off suppressed 2') RGC is characterized by a high baseline activity that is strongly suppressed below baseline during light increments and displays increased activity during light decrements.
claims.source: To our surprise, this was only the case for two types: (1) G32 ('Off suppressed 2') RGC, which is characterized by a high baseline activity that is strongly suppressed below baseline during light increments and displays increased activity during light decrements, and (2) G18, which is considered as being a 'Fast On' type having a response to light increments with a fast response kinetic.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the functional properties of G32 RGCs.

claims.claim: G18 is considered as being a 'Fast On' type having a response to light increments with a fast response kinetic.
claims.source: To our surprise, this was only the case for two types: (1) G32 ('Off suppressed 2') RGC, which is characterized by a high baseline activity that is strongly suppressed below baseline during light increments and displays increased activity during light decrements, and (2) G18, which is considered as being a 'Fast On' type having a response to light increments with a fast response kinetic.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the functional properties of G18 RGCs.

claims.claim: The chirp stimulus was subdivided into six feature segments: On, Off, low frequency, high frequency, low contrast, and high contrast.
claims.source: To this end, we subdivided the chirp stimulus into six feature segments ((1) On, (2) Off, (3) low frequency, (4) high frequency, (5) low contrast, (6) high contrast), and the moving bar into two ((7) On, (8) Off) (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis approach for dissecting stimulus responses, shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: The moving bar stimulus was subdivided into two feature segments: On and Off.
claims.source: To this end, we subdivided the chirp stimulus into six feature segments ((1) On, (2) Off, (3) low frequency, (4) high frequency, (5) low contrast, (6) high contrast), and the moving bar into two ((7) On, (8) Off) (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis approach for dissecting stimulus responses, shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: Three response behaviors were found across RGC types: not NO-affected/stable, showing adaptational cell type-specific changes, and NO-affected.
claims.source: Through this analysis, we found three response behaviors across the RGC types: (1) not NO-affected/stable, (2) showing adaptational cell type-specific changes, and (3) NO-affected (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the feature-based analysis, shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: G32 showed barely any adaptational response changes, yet its activity increased during NO application.
claims.source: As before, we found that G32 is strongly affected by NO; it showed barely any adaptational response changes, yet its activity increased during NO application (Figure 4b, (3)).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the feature-based analysis, shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The increase in G32 activity was statistically significant for the chirp's On and Off steps and during both the frequency and contrast modulations, as well as for the moving bar's trailing edge.
claims.source: This increase in activity was statistically significant for the chirp's On (1) and Off steps (2) and during both the frequency and contrast modulations ((3)–(6)), as well as for the moving bars trailing edge (8) (for tests, see Figure 4 legend), suggesting that NO reduces the cell's inhibition by temporal contrast.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the feature-based analysis, with details in Figure 4.

claims.claim: NO reduces G32's inhibition by temporal contrast.
claims.source: This increase in activity was statistically significant for the chirp's On (1) and Off steps (2) and during both the frequency and contrast modulations ((3)–(6)), as well as for the moving bars trailing edge (8) (for tests, see Figure 4 legend), suggesting that NO reduces the cell's inhibition by temporal contrast.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings about G32 responses.

claims.claim: G31 ('Off suppressed 1') displayed a similar behavior to G32 during NO application.
claims.source: Interestingly, a cell type from the same larger functional group that features analogous response properties, G31 ('Off suppressed 1'), displayed a similar behavior during the NO application (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the feature-based analysis, shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: G31 showed response changes for most features already in the control, suggesting that this effect was primarily adaptational.
claims.source: However, G31 showed this response change for most features already in the control, suggesting that this effect was primarily adaptational (Figure 4a, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing control and NO effects in G31, shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: In G31, the response to the chirp's Off step increased with NO, whereas that to the moving bar's leading edge decreased.
claims.source: Still, our analysis suggests that NO had a significant effect, though different from what we observed for G32: in G31 the response to the chirp's Off step (2) increased, whereas that to the moving bar's leading edge (7) decreased.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the feature-based analysis of G31 responses.

claims.claim: Additional NO effects on G31 may have been 'masked' by the strong adaptational response changes.
claims.source: Note that it is possible that additional NO effects on G31 may have been 'masked' by the strong adaptational response changes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations in detecting NO effects in G31.

claims.claim: G18 showed significant differences between the control- and NO-dataset in the initial analysis, but this effect was not mirrored by the feature-wise analysis.

claims.claim: Adaptational and NO-induced effects occurred on a feature-specific as well as cell type-specific level.

claims.claim: G32 likely contains three distinct response types – all suppressed-by-contrast (SbC) but to different degrees.

claims.claim: G32 may consist of three SbC RGC types and in at least two of them, the contrast suppression is strongly modulated by NO.

claims.claim: RGC responses to binary dense noise were recorded following the same experimental paradigm as for temporal responses.

claims.source: Next, we computed their sRFs for both recording conditions (Figure 6a) using spike-triggered averaging (Chichilnisky, 2001), obtaining control and NO sRFs, and then fitted a Gaussian to each sRF's center (Figure 6a).

claims.claim: The analysis focused on RGC types with reliable sRF estimates.

claims.claim: NO did not cause significant differences in surround strength for any of the analyzed RGC types.

claims.evidence: This is a finding from the surround index analysis.

claims.claim: G32 did not show NO-mediated differences in its sRF properties.

claims.claim: NO may only affect G32's temporal response, but not its RF organization.

claims.claim: For the tested RGC types, NO did not cause significant effects on sRF center size or surround strength.
claims.source: Taken together, at least for the tested RGC types, we did not detect any significant NO effects neither on sRF center size nor surround strength.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the receptive field analysis.

claims.claim: Two-photon imaging is limited by having a low temporal resolution to capture subtle temporal response dynamics.
claims.source: The high spatial resolution of two-photon imaging allowed us to record and identify individual RGCs. However, it is limited by having a low temporal resolution to capture subtle temporal response dynamics, which led us to record a complementary dataset using MEA recordings.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of two-photon imaging.

claims.claim: MEA recordings enabled investigation of subtle neuromodulatory effects with higher temporal resolution.
claims.source: Since we found that the temporal response domain of G32 and its subtypes were affected by NO, MEA recordings enabled us to further investigate subtle neuromodulatory effects with a higher temporal resolution.
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for using MEA recordings as a complementary approach.

claims.claim: Light-induced RGC responses (n=391) were recorded from four retinae under three consecutive conditions: control, NO-donor (DETA/NO; 100 µM), and wash-out.
claims.source: In particular, we recorded light-induced RGC responses (n=391) from four retinae under three consecutive conditions similar to the Ca2+-dataset: (1) control, (2) NO-donor (DETA/NO; 100 µM), and (3) wash-out.
claims.evidence: This describes the MEA experimental design.

claims.claim: The chirp stimulus was used for type identification and a checkerboard stimulus was used to estimate RFs in the MEA dataset.
claims.source: As for the Ca2+-dataset, we used the chirp stimulus for type identification as well as a checkerboard stimulus to estimate RFs.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the MEA experiments.

claims.claim: RGC responses were clustered across retinae and spike trains were transformed into pseudo-calcium traces to match with RGC types from Baden et al., 2016.
claims.source: To identify and compare RGC types across the Ca2+- and MEA-dataset, we clustered the RGC responses across retinae (Figure 7a and b) and transformed their spike trains in response to the chirp stimulus into pseudo-calcium traces as described in Goldin et al., 2022 (Figure 7c; see Methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis approach for matching MEA and Ca2+ datasets, shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Responses from all known RGC types were recorded in the MEA dataset, yet the sampling fractions for most types differ between the datasets.
claims.source: Overall, we were able to record responses from all known RGC types, yet the sampling fractions for most types differ between the datasets, which can be explained by the recording bias inherent in MEA (Trapani et al., 2023; Figure 7f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing the MEA and Ca2+ datasets, shown in Figure 7f.

claims.claim: The difference in sampling fractions between datasets can be explained by the recording bias inherent in MEA.
claims.source: Overall, we were able to record responses from all known RGC types, yet the sampling fractions for most types differ between the datasets, which can be explained by the recording bias inherent in MEA (Trapani et al., 2023; Figure 7f).
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the observed differences, supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: G32 showed reduced suppression during NO application in the MEA dataset, similar to the Ca2+ dataset.
claims.source: We found that, similar to the Ca2+-dataset (Figure 5), G32 showed reduced suppression during NO application (Figure 8a, top), which was not present anymore in the recording after wash-out, indicating that the NO-induced effect may be reversible (Figure 8a, bottom).

claims.claim: The NO-induced effect on G32 was not present anymore in the recording after wash-out, indicating that the effect may be reversible.
claims.source: We found that, similar to the Ca2+-dataset (Figure 5), G32 showed reduced suppression during NO application (Figure 8a, top), which was not present anymore in the recording after wash-out, indicating that the NO-induced effect may be reversible (Figure 8a, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the MEA experiments with wash-out, shown in Figure 8a.

claims.claim: The same clustering approach applied to the Ca2+ dataset revealed three clusters in the electrically recorded RGCs assigned to G32.
claims.source: Since we found in our Ca2+-dataset that G32 consists of three subtypes, we applied the same clustering approach to the electrically recorded RGCs assigned to G32, revealing also three clusters (Figure 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis of MEA data, shown in Figure 8b.

claims.claim: For all three G32 clusters in the MEA dataset, NO-induced response modulations were found but to varying degrees.
claims.source: For all three clusters, we found NO-induced response modulations but to varying degrees.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the three G32 clusters in the MEA dataset.

claims.claim: The NO effects on G32 clusters were at least partially reversible.

claims.evidence: This is a finding from the wash-out experiments, shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: For all three G32 clusters, an increase in cumulative firing rate during DETA/NO application was found for at least one feature.
claims.source: We found for all three clusters an increase in cumulative firing rate during DETA/NO application – indicative of a reduction in suppression – for at least one feature (Figure 8—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spike rate analysis, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: The NO effect was differential between G32 clusters, further supporting the presence of multiple RGC types in G32.
claims.source: That the NO effect was differential (e.g. compare 'Freq. step' and 'On step' between clusters) further supports the presence of multiple RGC types in G32.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential NO effects across clusters.

claims.claim: NO did not induce modulation of sRF size in any of the G32 clusters in the MEA dataset.
claims.source: In line with the Ca2+-dataset, we did not find any NO-induced modulation of sRF size in any of the clusters (Figure 8d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the MEA receptive field analysis, shown in Figure 8d.

claims.claim: The temporal RF (tRF) kernels showed significantly faster response kinetics during NO application for all three G32 clusters.
claims.source: However, the temporal RF (tRF) kernels showed significantly faster response kinetics during NO application for all three clusters (Figure 8e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the temporal RF analysis, shown in Figure 8e.

claims.claim: The effects on temporal RF kinetics were reversible for two clusters (except for cluster iii).

claims.evidence: This is a finding from the wash-out analysis of temporal RFs.

claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the difference between Ca2+ and MEA findings.

claims.claim: The G32 subtypes identified in both datasets do not necessarily correspond to the same RGC types.
claims.source: Note that the G32 subtypes identified in both datasets do not necessarily correspond to the same RGC types: While two clusters show high correlations between Ca2+ and MEA-data (clusters 2 vs. ii, 3 vs. i), one clearly differs in its temporal response (cluster 1 vs. iii; Figure 8—figure supplement 3a and b; see also Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a caveat about comparing clusters across datasets, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The MEA-dataset confirms that G32 consists of three subtypes and that their temporal responses are modulated by NO.
claims.source: Taken together, our MEA-dataset confirms that G32 consists of three subtypes and that their temporal responses are modulated by NO: it reduced their suppression by temporal contrast.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the MEA experiments.

claims.claim: NO reduced suppression by temporal contrast in G32 subtypes.
claims.source: Taken together, our MEA-dataset confirms that G32 consists of three subtypes and that their temporal responses are modulated by NO: it reduced their suppression by temporal contrast.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the MEA experiments.

claims.claim: All three G32 subtypes displayed faster response kinetics under NO, an effect that was reversible.
claims.source: Additionally, the analysis of the MEA-dataset (tRF) revealed that all three subtypes displayed faster response kinetics under NO, an effect that was reversible.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the MEA temporal RF analysis.

claims.claim: The sRFs of G32 subtypes were unchanged by NO, in line with the Ca2+ data.

claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the MEA spatial RF analysis.

claims.claim: nNOS-2 AC releases NO in response to flickering light (fast changes in contrast).
claims.source: In particular, it releases NO in response to flickering light (i.e. fast changes in contrast) (Blom et al., 2012; Eldred and Blute, 2005; Jacoby et al., 2018; Vielma et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2007).

claims.claim: nNOS-2 ACs report fast contrast changes at photopic conditions.

claims.evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: G32 RGCs could relay contrast changes to higher visual targets.

claims.evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.evidence: This is a comparison to another study, supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: The set of visual stimuli was restricted to artificial ones to ensure reliable RGC type classification.

claims.evidence: This explains a methodological choice in the study.

claims.claim: Artificial stimuli probe the stimulus space in a rather selective and limited fashion.

claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claims.claim: Natural images or movies may be needed for a more complete picture of the functional implication of retinal neuromodulation.
claims.source: Specifically, natural images or movies – stimuli that are closer to what the retina evolved to process (Qiu et al., 2021) – may be needed for a more complete picture of the functional implication of retinal neuromodulation.
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future studies based on the study's limitations.

claims.claim: Natural stimuli can reveal novel nonlinear properties of retinal functions.

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: An RGC's contrast selectivity can be context-dependent.
claims.source: That natural stimuli can reveal novel nonlinear properties of retinal functions were demonstrated, for example, by Goldin et al., 2022, who showed that an RGC's contrast selectivity can be context-dependent.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: Transient SbC RGC (G28) features center color-opponent responses and may signal context changes.
claims.source: Similarly, Höfling et al., 2024, recorded natural movie-evoked RGC responses to train a convolutional neural network, which through in silico experiments allowed them to discover that transient SbC RGC (G28) feature center color-opponent responses and may signal context changes.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: Future studies on retinal neuromodulators should employ natural stimuli.

claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on cited studies.

claims.claim: The level of light adaptation is an important aspect to consider when studying NO neuromodulation in the retina.
claims.source: Another important aspect to consider when studying NO neuromodulation in the retina is the level of light adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about an important experimental consideration.

claims.claim: Several studies proposed that NO facilitates the transition across light levels.
claims.source: Several studies proposed that NO facilitates the transition across light levels (Mills and Massey, 1995; Snellman and Nawy, 2004; Tooker et al., 2013), especially to photopic conditions (Jacoby et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The experiments were performed in the low photopic range due to two-photon imaging resulting in a certain level of background 'illumination'.

claims.claim: NO-mediated neuromodulation may serve additional light-level dependent functions: more globally during the transition from scotopic to mesopic/photopic, and more cell type-specific in the photopic regime.
claims.source: Therefore, NO-mediated neuromodulation may serve additional light-level dependent functions: More globally during the transition from scotopic to mesopic/photopic, and more cell type-specific in the photopic regime, as we reported here.

claims.claim: Estimates for the endogenous NO concentration in the retina range from a few 100 nM at the RGCs to approximately 1 µM at the vitreous boundary.
claims.source: Estimates for the endogenous NO concentration in the retina range from a few 100 nM at the RGCs (Kalamkarov et al., 2016) to ∼1 µM at the vitreous boundary (Guthrie, 2014; Guthrie and Mieler, 2014).

claims.claim: The applied NO concentration results in a small to moderate NO increase within the measured physiological range.
claims.source: Therefore, the here applied concentration results in a small to moderate NO increase within the measured physiological range.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing the applied concentration to endogenous levels.

claims.claim: The fact that the applied NO concentration resulted in a clear, type-specific effect argues for NO having a potent neuromodulatory effect on the retinal output.
claims.source: The fact that this already resulted in a clear, type-specific effect, argues for NO having a potent neuromodulatory effect on the retinal output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: DETA/NO itself may affect the electrical properties of cultured cerebellar granule cells by reversibly activating cation-selective channels, independent of NO.
claims.source: It has been reported for DETA/NO that the donor itself – independent of NO – may affect the electrical properties of cultured cerebellar granule cells by reversibly activating a cation-selective channels (Thompson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: Side-effects of DETA/NO are unlikely to have substantially contributed to the effects observed in G32 RGCs because substantial side-effects were mainly observed at much higher DETA/NO concentrations (3 mM).
claims.source: While we cannot exclude that this side-effect of DETA/NO may have contributed to the effects we observed in G32 RGCs, we consider this unlikely, because substantial side-effects were mainly observed by Thompson et al., 2009, at much higher DETA/NO concentrations (3 mM) than we used in our study.
claims.evidence: This is an argument against a potential confound, based on comparing concentrations to a cited study.

claims.claim: RGC types referred to as 'SbC' are characterized by a decrease in their activity for both positive and negative temporal contrasts within their RF.
claims.source: Functionally, RGC types referred to as 'SbC' are characterized by a decrease in their activity for both positive and negative temporal contrasts within their RF (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2018; Jacoby et al., 2015; Tien et al., 2016; Tien et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: In Baden et al., 2016, three functional RGC types were labeled SbC based on their light stimulus-evoked Ca2+ response being suppressed primarily by positive (On-SbC: G28) or negative temporal contrast (Off-SbCs: G31, G32).
claims.source: In Baden et al., 2016, three functional RGC types were labeled SbC based on their light stimulus-evoked Ca2+ response being suppressed primarily by positive (On-SbC: G28) or negative temporal contrast (Off-SbCs: G31, G32).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on a cited reference.

claims.claim: G32 is also suppressed by the moving bar stimulus, suggesting that the cells are also sensitive to spatial contrast.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Coverage analysis indicated that G32 may contain several RGC types.
claims.source: Coverage analysis indicated that G32 may contain several RGC types (Baden et al., 2016) – in line with our cluster analysis.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on a cited reference and is consistent with the current study's findings.

claims.claim: It is unclear if G32 contains one or more of the individually studied SbC types in mouse.
claims.source: It is still unclear if G32 contains one (or more) of the individually studied SbC types in mouse (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2018; Tien et al., 2016; Tien et al., 2015; Wienbar and Schwartz, 2022), yet, recently, Goetz et al., 2022, speculated if the novel bursty-SbC RGC (Wienbar and Schwartz, 2022) aligns with (a sub-cluster of) G32.

claims.claim: Goetz et al., 2022, speculated if the novel bursty-SbC RGC aligns with a sub-cluster of G32.
claims.source: It is still unclear if G32 contains one (or more) of the individually studied SbC types in mouse (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2018; Tien et al., 2016; Tien et al., 2015; Wienbar and Schwartz, 2022), yet, recently, Goetz et al., 2022, speculated if the novel bursty-SbC RGC (Wienbar and Schwartz, 2022) aligns with (a sub-cluster of) G32.
